Theme

Conversation, family & daily routines

by Hercules! interjection

the oaths

also honestly, upon my word, I swear, by golly, by Jove, heavens!, geez, gee, honest to god, honest to goodness, heavens no

classical

Plaut. Cas. 801b: Ēsuriō hercle
Ter. Ph. 386: Periī hercle: nōmen perdidī.
Traupman 320

1Gell. 11.6.1 (and Charisius): in the old writers Roman women do not swear by Hercules, nor men by Castor; edepol is common to both. Lewis & Short (s.v. Castor) finds ēcastor “especially by women, though not exclusively by them”. The plays bear the rule out on the whole (loci-plautus).

hercle1

interjection; anywhere in the clause, often after its first word · Wiktionary

by Hercules! honestly!

(vōx cōmica et sermōnis cotīdiānī: Plaut., Ter.)

The vocative of Herculēs. A man’s oath.

Other words

  • mehercule (mehercle, mehercules) — by Hercules! truly

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 2.5.2: sed mehercule nē, cum vēneris, nōn habeās jam quod cūrēs · Wiktionary

    (Cic. in epistulīs)

    The form of Cicero’s letters, where hercle is rare.

  • edepol1, pol — by Pollux! indeed

    also used · classical · Ter. Ph. 1053: Pol vērō vocō.; Plaut. Most. 376: Quaesō edepol, exsurge; pater advenit.; Traupman 98: eu edepol, eu hercle, geez; Traupman 43; Traupman 327 · Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; pol also Hor.)

    Said by men and women alike (Gellius).

  • ēcastor1, mēcastor — by Castor! (a woman’s oath)

    also used · classical · Plaut. Amph. 508: Ēcastor tē experior quantī faciās uxōrem tuam.; Plaut. Cas. 171: Salvē mēcastor. · Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.)

    Mostly women’s speech.

  • medius fidius — so help me God! as true as heaven!

    also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 5.21.1: ūnum medius fidius tēcum diem libentius posuerim; Traupman 108; Traupman 100: honest to god

    (Cic. in epistulīs; Sall., Plin. Ep.)

    Lewis & Short (s.v. Fidius): an oath by the god of good faith, “as true as heaven!”; also written as one word.

Examples

  • Quid agis, mea salūs? — Ēsuriō hercle, atque adeō hau salūbriter.

    How are you, my darling? — Starving, by Hercules, and not in a healthy way.Plaut. Cas. 801–801b

  • Periī hercle: nōmen perdidī.

    Heavens, I’m done for: I’ve forgotten the name.Ter. Ph. 386

  • sed mehercule nē, cum vēneris, nōn habeās jam quod cūrēs

    but, honestly, I fear that when you come you’ll have nothing left to look afterCic. Fam. 2.5.2

  • Mē ad cēnam vocā. — Pol vērō vocō.

    Invite me to dinner. — I do indeed invite you.Ter. Ph. 1053

  • Ēcastor tē experior quantī faciās uxōrem tuam.

    Truly, I find out how much you value your wife.Plaut. Amph. 508

  • ūnum medius fidius tēcum diem libentius posuerim quam hoc omne tempus cum plērīsque eōrum, quibuscum vīvō necessāriō

    so help me, I would rather spend one day with you than all this time with most of those I have to live withCic. Fam. 5.21.1

  • Minimē hercle!

    Heavens, no!Cic. Lael. 30 (Lewis & Short)

  • Minimē, hercle.

    Heavens, no!Traupman 138

  • Eu edepol! Eu hercle!

    Geez!Traupman 320

See also good heavens!, truly, really?.
